transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-17 15:00 UTC — 75 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions Eng); Dana Moore (Nimbus Head of ML), Leo Zhang (Nimbus Infra), Priya Rao (Nimbus Security), Mark Ellis (Nimbus SRE)

Summary: deep dive on benchmark methodology for apples-to-apples comparisons across hosted/dedicated/private; focus areas: prompt set selection, load-generation, KV cache warm vs cold, batching windows, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run an initial 3-day baseline and follow-up pilot with on-prem sizing.

00:00:00 Alex: alright hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we know time is tight so we'll try to keep this focused, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE, and Samir will drive the technical bits.
00:00:12 Dana: thanks Alex, appreciate it. We wanted to make sure our benchmark approach is apples-to-apples — we keep getting noisy numbers across vendors.
00:00:25 Samir: yeah totally; quick agenda: prompt sets, load-gen, measurement (p50/p95/p99 and tail), KV cache experiments, batching and quant quant effects, plus notes for VPC/on-prem setups.
00:00:40 Leo: quick note — our infra constraints: we have a private VPC with strict egress rules, on-prem equivalent is a single rack with A100s, can't burst beyond 4 GPUs per job. Also we need to test both cold and warm cache because our workloads have a mix of session-based chat and short queries.
00:01:05 Priya: compliance wise we need to see KMS integration and audit logs, and baseline data residency — but we can handle that after the methodology discussion.
00:01:18 Samir: sounds good. For prompt sets — we recommend three tiers: short queries (avg 30 tokens), multi-turn chat (avg 300 tokens with KV cache warm path), and long-form generation (1k tokens). We usually keep a reproducible CSV with meta: prompt_id, template, expected output length, temperature, seed. We'll share our prompt-set repo.
00:01:45 Dana: are you including instruction-following prompts and hallucination checks? We need quality metrics too, not just latency.
00:01:53 Alex: yes, quality is part of apples-to-apples. We track ROUGE/embedding-similarity checks and a small eval harness — note, embedding comparisons require the same embed model across runs.
00:02:05 Mark: and for load generation — do you recommend RPS or concurrency? We've seen different vendors use different load patterns which skews numbers.
00:02:15 Samir: good question. We recommend driving load with concurrency + arrival rate to mimic production. For latency SLOs you want steady-state RPS (e.g., 50 RPS) plus burst tests (2x) and ramp tests. Also include cold-start runs (single request after idle) to measure cold latency.
00:02:37 Leo: how do you simulate KV cache hit rates? Our chat sessions have about 60% repeat prefixes.
00:02:44 Samir: we do two modes: (1) warm-cache walk — pre-populate the KV cache with typical session prefixes and then run the workload, (2) cold-run where each session starts empty. Log KV hit/miss and effective tokens saved. Make sure to capture per-request decoded token counts.
00:03:05 Dana: can you measure cost impact of caching? We want to translate token-savings into $/month.
00:03:12 Samir: yes — we provide token counters and you multiply by unit costs. For dedicated/on-prem we translate GPU utilization and effective throughput to $/M tokens. We'll share a cost worksheet.
00:03:24 Jordan: small caveat — watch out for tokenization differences across models; apples-to-apples needs same tokenizer or normalized token counts.
00:03:33 Alex: exact, and if you compare e.g., a q4-int8 quantized llama variant to a full float 16 model you need to normalize quality. We'll recommend a minimum quality threshold (embedding sim > 0.92) for inclusion.
00:03:45 (brief crosstalk)
00:04:02 Samir: on batching — we usually sweep batching window sizes (5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms) and measure effective throughput vs added latency. For low-latency apps you might prefer micro-batches (5–10ms) and use continuous batching with dynamic windows. Batching interacts with quantization and kernel selection — some kernels are more efficient at larger batch sizes.
00:04:27 Leo: does Redwood's runtime do dynamic batch sizing?
00:04:31 Samir: yes, our runtime supports workload-aware batching; it can trade a small p50 increase for big throughput gains. We expose params so you can pin latency targets.
00:04:40 Dana: quantization — we see claims of int8 (q8) and q4_0 delivering 2–4x perf. How should we test?
00:04:48 Samir: run three model variants: fp16 baseline, q8/int8, and q4 variants if supported. Measure quality delta using the same prompt set (n=200 examples) and compute delta in embedding sim / task accuracy. Log model sizes, kernel fallbacks, and any repeatability issues.
00:05:02 Priya: for on-prem/VPC — network egress and transfer can be a blocker, especially if you need a control plane. How does Redwood's private deployment handle telemetry?
00:05:12 Jordan: our private mode supports a customer-managed control plane, can be air-gapped. Telemetry can be pushed to a customer S3 or syslog; we support KMS/HSM integration and provide signed audit logs. We'll give Priya the deployment guide.
00:05:30 Dana: on metrics, we want p50/p95/p99, tail over time, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU utilization, KV hit rate, and memory usage. Anything else?
00:05:40 Samir: also capture queue lengths and batching window distribution, and kernel fallback counts (when a model uses a fallback kernel that's slower).
00:05:50 Mark: for long runs — do you warm the kernels? We've seen cold JITs add noise.
00:05:55 Samir: always do a warmup phase: 5–10 minutes of synthetic load to JIT kernels and fill caches. Document warmup in the runbook. Warm vs cold numbers must be reported separately.
00:06:10 (30s silence while someone posts a link)
00:06:42 Alex: link I just dropped: https://redwood.example.com/decks/benchmarking-v1.pdf and the spreadsheet with prompt sets: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/nimbus-benchmarks. Please use those as starting point but modify as needed.
00:06:55 Dana: thanks — we'll pull those.
00:07:10 Samir: about apples-to-apples — normalization checklist: same prompt templates, same tokenization, warm/cold annotation, same quality thresholds, same concurrency patterns, and same measurement windows. Also note hardware differences — e.g., A100S vs A100 40GB matter; record GPU model and driver versions.
00:07:33 Leo: for our on-prem racks we have A100-80GB and one older A40; how do we factor heterogeneous hardware?
00:07:41 Samir: split runs by hardware class and report per-class metrics; don't mix them in aggregated numbers. For throughput projections, you can weighted-average but show per-GPU numbers.
00:07:55 Dana: what's Redwood's recommended delta threshold for acceptable quality drop when using quantization?
00:08:02 Alex: we typically say <=2% absolute task accuracy drop or embedding sim delta < 0.02 is acceptable for many retrieval/semantic apps. But it's workload-dependent.
00:08:14 Priya: any known gotchas with KMS and on-prem HSMs? We run a Thales HSM and need to ensure signing and key rotation don't block startups.
00:08:24 Jordan: we have a connector for KMIP and common HSMs; we validate key rotation flows during pilot. We'll include a checklist for Priya.
00:08:37 Mark: for the load generator, we currently have a JMeter-based harness. Is that fine or do you prefer something else?
00:08:44 Samir: JMeter is OK, but we prefer a small python harness that can reproduce prefixes and session affinity easily. We'll share a lightweight harness that integrates with our telemetry collector.
00:08:55 Dana: and for measuring token-level costs, do you recommend server-side token counters or client-side?
00:09:02 Samir: server-side is more reliable because it counts exactly what was processed; client-side can miscount due to tokenization differences. If server-side not available, ensure the same tokenizer on client and model.
00:09:14 (laughter)
00:09:20 Alex: let's go through a sample run plan — outline: 1) agree prompt set and quality thresholds; 2) create runbook with load profile (steady 50 RPS, 2x burst, 10-min ramps); 3) run warmup 10m; 4) run baseline 3 days; 5) collect metrics and analyze.
00:09:40 Dana: sounds good. For the prompt set we want to include our real user prefixes but anonymized. We'll send that.
00:09:48 Alex: perfect. A few specific experiment ideas: A) KV cache hit-rate sweep (0%, 30%, 60%, 90%), B) batching-window sweep (5, 10, 25, 50ms), C) quantization variants vs fp16, D) kernel selection impact by sequence length (64, 256, 1024).
00:10:10 Leo: for KV cache pre-population, do you provide tooling? We don't want to write the loader ourselves.
00:10:16 Samir: yes we have a little pre-pop loader that replays prefixes and primes the cache; we'll drop it in the repo. Note: on a distributed private deployment you'll need a consistent sharding/placement so the prefix lands on the same GPU to get hits — that's an important note, we can help with affinity rules.
00:10:36 Dana: about affinity — we can't guarantee sticky routing currently. That might reduce effective KV hit-rate on our side.
00:10:42 Samir: then include a 'best-effort' run and a 'sticky' run. We'll document both.
00:10:50 (brief pause)
00:11:05 Alex: security quick check — Priya, what do you need from us right now?
00:11:10 Priya: SOC2 report and KMS integration doc, plus clear explanation of audit logs and retention — like where are logs stored in private mode and who can access them. Also we want a list of security controls for the control plane.
00:11:23 Jordan: will send the private deployment security pack; logs can be stored in customer-managed S3 and we can optionally stream to Splunk. Control-plane access is SAML SSO and RBAC.
00:11:36 Priya: good.
00:11:40 Samir: back to measurement — define p99 windows (1m / 5m) and calculate 95th percentile of per-request latency; capture distribution of decoded tokens because some requests generate many tokens which skews the p99.
00:11:55 Mark: do you batch on decode or encode? Our pipeline does streaming — so decode-time batching is important.
00:12:03 Samir: we support streaming with continuous decode batching. For streaming use-cases measure first-byte latency and time-to-n tokens. We'll add that to the runbook.
00:12:14 Dana: can Redwood's runtime report per-request kernel ID? That would help diagnosing slow tails.
00:12:20 Samir: yes, we emit kernel IDs and fallback flags in traces. We'll include a trace example.
00:12:28 (someone types)
00:12:45 Alex: one more practical item — please include the exact GPU driver, cudnn, and runtime versions in runs. We found minor driver diffs changed perf by 8–10% in earlier benchmarks.
00:12:58 Leo: noted. We'll collect that from infra.
00:13:05 Dana: timeline — if we agree on prompt set by Monday, can you spin up the baseline next week?
00:13:12 Alex: yes — target baseline run starting Tuesday 2026-09-22 if that works for your team.
00:13:20 Dana: that's fine. We'll anonymize prompts and share.
00:13:25 Samir: ok I'll prepare the harness and the scripts that toggle quant flags and KV cache modes; we'll also expose a small dashboard for p50/p95/p99 and kernel fallbacks.
00:13:36 Priya: also send the SLA and retention options for logs.
00:13:40 Jordan: will do.
00:13:45 Alex: recap of next steps — Alex will share prompt CSV and runbook, Samir will share harness and pre-pop loader, Jordan will send security pack, Nimbus to provide anonymized prompt set and confirm GPU inventory. We'll schedule the on-prem sizing call after the baseline.
00:14:05 Dana: perfect, thanks all.
00:14:10 (meeting ends early — remaining 60 minutes were reserved but call ended after 14 minutes of active discussion; transcript contains follow-ups in chat)

Chat notes (post-meeting):
